title: Being My Parents' Translator | Legacy Project
description:
Irene Yoo is a food content creator, award-winning author of Soju Party, and co-owner of Orion Bar in Brooklyn, New York. Born in Detroit to immigrant parents who arrived in Michigan for graduate school, Irene and her family moved through Long Island and Alabama before settling in the suburbs of Southern California’s San Fernando Valley. As the eldest daughter, she early on assumed many of the de facto roles which came with being a cultural interpreter for her parents: translator, communicator, and surrogate caretaker for her younger sister. 

Between Korean school and church, she recalls spending weekends at Koreatown to shop at the Korean grocery stores, and rent VHS K-dramas with her mother. After moving to New York for college (fully intending to California!), Irene began a career in corporate food media, working as a Director and Producer for Food Network and Magnolia Network, the latter which she helped launch. 

Wondering why the foods familiar to her from her childhood weren’t being represented, she carved her own spaces to tell gastronomic stories. From doing pop-ups, opening the pocha-style Orion Bar, to writing a James Beard Award-winning cookbook, Irene hopes that her food brings comfort and inspires sonmat for those who encounter it; in her words, “we just made the bar that we wanted to go to all the time.”

title: Content Creator Jaeki Cho Receives the 2026 Trailblazer Award | Korean American Story
description:
Trailblazer Honoree Jaeki Cho shares how Korean American representation goes beyond visibility to building community with those around us.

Jaeki Cho (he/him) is a Korean American content creator and founder of Righteous Eats. After working as a magazine editor and writer, he built his career through filmmaking and digital storytelling. His work has reached billions of views by documenting overlooked stories–from neighborhood restaurants in Queens to communities around the world. Through every project, Jaeki hopes to inspire curiosity, foster empathy, and encourage people to see the world through someone else’s perspective.

This speech was delivered at the 16th Annual Korean American Story Gala, celebrating 16 years of sharing and preserving Korean American stories.

title: Adoptee Organizer Hollee McGinnis Receives the 2026 Trailblazer Award | Korean American Story
description:
Trailblazer Honoree Hollee McGinnis delivers an inspiring speech about how the hardships and challenges lead us to discover who we’re also known as.

Hollee A. McGinnis, Ph.D., MSW (she/her), also-known-as Lee Hwa Young, was adopted from South Korea and has almost 30 years of community organizing, practice, policy, and research experience relating to adoption and child welfare. Her work centers the lived experiences of individuals raised in alternative care (adoptive, foster and/or orphanages) so they can thrive across the lifespan and inform socially just child welfare policies and practices. Dr. McGinnis’ research focuses on adoptive and racial/ethnic identity, adverse childhood experiences/ complex trauma, cultural loss, the life course of adoption, and adoptee-led mutual aid groups. In 1996 she founded Also-Known-As, Inc., a non-profit adult intercountry adoptee organization in NYC.

This speech was delivered at the 16th Annual Korean American Story Gala, celebrating 16 years of sharing and preserving Korean American stories.

description:
Trailblazer Honoree Ali Ahn shares her journey of stubornly forging her own path on becoming an actor and inspiring others.

Ali Ahn (she/her) is an actor, recovering classical pianist, and native Los Angeleno. Please forgive her. She is currently starring opposite Keri Russell in The Diplomat and most recently appeared in the film Take Me Home. title: How Do You Celebrate Chuseok?
description:
Chuseok (추석) falls between September 24th and September 26th of the 2026 calendrical year. As the culmination of the harvest cycle, this autumn festival is a cherished time for loved ones to gather, share food, stories, and company, observing the turning of the seasons under full harvest moon as the days grow shorter and nights longer.

At the heart of the holiday is charye (차례), ancestral memorial rites where families prepare and offer freshly harvested crops, fruits, and traditional foods to honor their forebears. Households traditionally spend days preparing holiday treats like songpyeon (송편), stuffed rice cakes in the form of a half-moon, shaped with the wish for a bright future. Families also engage in beolcho (벌초), clearing weeds from ancestral gravesites ahead of the holiday.

As Korean Americans, Chuseok serves as a  reminder of the blessings of the year and of those who came before who paved the way for our communities to exist today. From Korean American Story, we wish everyone a happy Chuseok! 즐거운 한가위 되세요!

title: Finding Each Other Later in Life: Three Korean Adoptees Reflect | Through The Fog  #adoptionjourney
description:
Gathered for our final interview in New York for Through the Fog, and together in candid reflection, Sarah, Laura, and Joy map the winding and disorienting terrain of coming into the Korean American adoptee community later in life.

 Tracing their connection back to the 2025 Korean American Adoptee Network Conference in Atlanta, Joy recalls feeling pulled by the sisters’ lightness, initiating a relationship she describes as “hitting the lottery.” For Joy, who grew up as the only Asian child in a predominantly white Long Island town, and for Sarah and Laura, who spent decades feeling unanchored within their missionary upbringing in Seoul, finding each other offered a rare sanctuary.

A central thread of their dialogue dives into the visceral toll of adoption trauma, the somatic release of stored grief, and the evolving relationship with their pasts. Joy reflects on the overwhelming emotional weight of her past return to Korea (spending five months volunteering at the orphanage where she had been placed) while Laura speaks to the meaningful yet destabilizing reunion with a biological sister after 53 years. In shedding the exhaustive negotiations of "fitting in" vs. “belonging,” of tethering and anchoring affects, and cultivating spaces of unpretentious, mutual belonging, they affirm how community plays a critical in honoring ongoing practices of self-compassion, where recognition becomes its own language for mourning and healing.

Special thanks to the Thomas and Wonsook Foundation for their generous support in making this project possible. And to Joy Lieberthal Rho, founder of IAMAdoptee for her consultation and post-support services for this project.

title: Raised in Korea, But Still an Outsider | Through The Fog
description:
Laura Underwood was born in Seoul in 1972 and adopted as an infant into the prominent Underwood family, whose missionary legacy in Korea dates back five generations to 1885. Raised by fluent Korean-speaking parents, she grew up immersed in a unique world while feeling like an outsider who didn’t look like the rest of her family. Though surrounded by Korean culture, she was excluded from the language and details of her own origins, instead raised on an adoption narrative shaped by faith and fate. For decades, she felt unanchored from her identity as a Korean adoptee.

In adulthood, Laura and her non-biological sister Sarah submitted their DNA to 23andMe in 2019, eventually leading Laura to discover and meet her biological sister in 2025. Finding detailed adoption records from Incheon helped her challenge the narratives she had inherited and reclaim a sense of agency. Through the Korean American Adoptee Adoptive Family Network (KAAN), she found community and solidarity, embracing the complexity of her story and the understanding that the story Laura has to tell today, is “not the same story that [she] was taught.”

Special thanks to the Thomas and Wonsook Foundation for their generous support in making this project possible. And to Joy Lieberthal Rho, founder of IAMAdoptee for her consultation and post-support services for this project.

title: Raised in Korea, But Not Taught Korean | Through The Fog #adoption
description:
Sarah Weber was born in Seoul in 1973 and adopted by an American missionary family who had lived in Korea for generations. The youngest of four, she was raised in Seoul by parents who spoke fluent Korean, noting that her father’s family had lived in Korea for four generations, beginning with the first arrival of Presbyterian missionary (H.G. Underwood) to Incheon in 1885. Despite growing up surrounded by Korean culture – Sarah felt largely disconnected from it, attending international schools and an English-speaking church without learning the Korean language.  She describes the painful irony of standing silently beside her fluent white mother in Korean markets, and realizing her parents sometimes used Korean to speak privately —“weaponizing my own language against me.” Though adoption was openly acknowledged in her family, they never discussed the complexities of growing up as a transracial adoptee.

After moving to the United States for college, Sarah spent years outside the adoptee community before finding connection in Michigan and beginning to unpack the systemic structures behind international adoption. Today, as the mother of an intercountry adoptee herself, Sarah hopes her daughter knows she will always provide a safe space for whenever she is ready to explore her own identity and experience on her own terms.

Special thanks to the Thomas and Wonsook Foundation for their generous support in making this project possible. And to Joy Lieberthal Rho, founder of IAMAdoptee for her consultation and post-support services for this project.

title: Motherhood as Adoptees: What We Carry | Through The Fog
description:
Alisha Bennett and Emily Flynn unpack the complex emotional landscape of motherhood after a lifetime shaped by early separation and, later, reconnection with their birth families. Reflecting on their own infant relinquishments, they explore how old survival mechanisms and an underlying fear of loss resurfaced during pregnancy and postpartum life.

Together, they confront the unique challenges of parenting as transracial adoptees, including the lack of language, support, and understanding around adoption-related trauma and postpartum depression. Through friendship, community, and insights from IKAA symposiums, Alisha and Emily have found ways to transform decades of unspoken grief into a more intentional, deeply present love for the next generation—and hope that sharing their experiences will help other adoptee parents feel less alone.

Special thanks to the Thomas and Wonsook Foundation for their generous support in making this project possible. title: How Shared Grief Brings Healing | Through The Fog #adoptionjourney
description:
Heather Schultz Gittens is a writer, educator, and cycle-breaker based in New York. Born in Seoul in 1984, she was adopted at four months old through Eastern Social Welfare (ESWS) and Love the Children in Pennsylvania and raised in Long Island. After enduring a long battle with multiple sclerosis, her mother passed away when she was ten. Heather received her mother’s childhood journal, which preserved memories of her early years and her parents’ efforts to honor her Korean heritage.

Following her mother’s passing, Heather endured family conflict, housing insecurity, and barriers to education. Even being told by her stepmother, “You’re not Korean, you’re American.” With her grandmother’s support, she earned a bachelor’s degree and MPA from Baruch College. In 2014, she returned to Seoul, revisiting ESWS and birth clinic while confronting the challenges of accessing her records.

Motherhood sparked a deeper journey of healing through somatic work and connection with other adoptees. A TEDx speaker and aspiring author of Korean folklore children's books, Heather channels her lived experience today by helping others to do the uncomfortable, yet rewarding, work of healing within their own lives.

Special thanks to the Thomas and Wonsook Foundation for their generous support in making this project possible. And to Joy Lieberthal Rho, founder of IAMAdoptee for her consultation and post-support services for this project.

In 2014, she returned to Seoul, revisiting ESWS and birth clinic while confronting the challenges of accessing her records.

Motherhood sparked a deeper journey of healing through somatic work and connection with other adoptees. A TEDx speaker and aspiring author of Korean folklore children's books, Heather channels her lived experience today by helping others to do the uncomfortable, yet rewarding, work of healing within their own lives.

title: Learning Not to Walk Alone as an Adoptee | Through The Fog
description:
Emily Flynn is a textile designer, field hockey enthusiast, and board member of Also-Known-As. Born in Seoul, she was adopted at five months old into a white family in New Jersey and raised in Vermont, where she grew up in a largely colorblind, predominantly white community. Without the language to express feeling othered, she spent years navigating hyper-vigilance and survival mode. Field hockey became a refuge, eventually leading her to play competitively in college and found NYC Field Hockey.

A study abroad trip to Italy challenged her sense of being “white-adjacent” when locals repeatedly addressed her in Asian languages, prompting a deeper exploration of her Korean identity. Becoming a mother strengthened that connection, inspiring her to incorporate Korean food, language, music, and heritage into her children’s lives. In 2019, she reunited with her birth mother, stepfather, and half-brother in Seoul after initiating a search through Social Welfare Society.

Alongside her husband, who is also an adoptee, Emily continues to explore the complexities of adoption, family, and identity. After losing her closest sibling—a fellow Korean adoptee, trans woman, and best friend—she turned her grief into purpose, dedicating herself to building healing spaces within the adoptee community through Also-Known-As and reminding others that they don’t have to walk alone.

title: I Made Fun of Myself Before Others Could As An Adoptee | Through The Fog
description:
Alisha Bennett, LCSW, is the founder and director of Integrative Therapy NYC. Born in Daegu, South Korea, in 1984, she was adopted at three months old by an American family in Michigan through Holt International. Growing up in a predominantly white, religious community, Alisha experienced racism and “othering” that shaped her relationship with her Korean identity into adulthood.

title: “They’re Not Making More of Us”: 30 Years of Adoptee Community | Through The Fog
description:
In a conversation spanning 30 years of nonprofit history, community building, and mentorship, four leaders (and former presidents!) of Also-Known-As share and reflect on their experience with guiding the organization, as well as what being in community with other international adoptees has taught them. At the heart of their conversation are service and mentorship, two foundational pillars of Also-Known-As when it was founded in 1996 by a small group of Korean adoptees in New York. Yet what began as a mentorship program has since blossomed into a nonprofit organization dedicated to empowering international adoptees from all backgrounds, with ongoing educational, cultural, and post-adoptive workshops that strives to build a space that celebrates the diverse and intersectional identities of the adult adoptee community.
 
Observing that the organization will continue to grow to meet the needs of international adoptees, Hollee McGinnis notes how she’s seen Also-Known-As evolve throughout the years in its commitment to planning social events where both mentors and mentees could learn from one another; likewise, Marissa Martin describes how Also-Known-As deepening its relationships with small businesses, the Korean consulate, and other organizations has helped expand Also-Known-As’ reach and visibility across different communities. Lindsay Geier, whose tenure marked the first time Also-Known-As had an international Chinese adoptee as President, recalls how she found within the organization a racial mirroring absent in the predominantly white community of many adoptees’ upbringing, hoping others can look to the organization’s board to reclaim their own stories. Referring to the end of international adoptions from Korea, Michael Mullen highlights that the years of advocacy and community-building undertaken by Korean adoptees should serve international adoptees from all backgrounds: “They’re not making more of us!”

title: An Adoptee’s Place in The Korean Diaspora | Through The Fog
description:
Marissa Martin, 43, is a nonprofit consultant and policy advocate who serves on the Advisory Board of Also-Known-As. Born in Incheon, South Korea, she was adopted when she was 6 months old by a family from New Hope, a small suburb just outside of Philadelphia. Growing up in a predominantly white neighborhood in the 1980s, Marissa recounts that while her parents did acknowledge her Korean heritage, adoption agencies often encouraged raising children in a “colorblind” environment; in fact, she tells us about how mother was quite involved with her adoption agency, frequenting Korea to bring back other babies, as well as textiles and hanbok.

When Marissa was 14, she discovered her adoption file, though she didn’t address the contents with her family: information about her birth parents and the circumstances of her adoption. Convinced that the only person she could rely on was herself, she left for college in D.C.. There she reached out to Holt to inquire about her file, where she received a bizarre set of non-identifying details about her birth parents. 

When Marissa was 25, she visited Korea for the first time, meeting her foster mother and visiting the agency which handled her adoption—an emotional experience left her conflicted on returning again. Since that initial visit, Marissa has been back to Korea ten times and is in reunion with her birth mother and relatives. Their relationship is calibrated by “some good meetings, and some terrible meetings,” giving narratives to complicated emotions as a crutch against grieving them. Yet throughout her life, she has embraced being a Korean adoptee, while still hoping that one day she can simply say, “I’m Korean American,” without the “adoptee” attached.

title: What Happens After Reunion: The Impact of Adoption | Through The Fog
description:
Hollee McGinnis is a professor, community organizer, and the founder of Also-Known-As, a non-profit adult intercountry adoptee organization based in New York City. Born in Incheon, South Korea, she was raised by her birth mother and paternal grandparents before being placed into an orphanage on Deokjeok Island, from which she was adopted at the age of 3½ by an Irish Catholic family from Westchester County. She returned to Korea when she as 24, reconnecting with “pieces” from her early life which lingered, in varying degrees of clarity, within her memory: the half-staircase of the split-level orphanage, the enduring love and affection of her foster parents who cared for her as a toddler. She also met with her biological family, from whom she learned of the socioeconomic pressures her birth mother, a factory worker, faced as a single parent, as well the efforts of her grandfather to keep her anchored to the family tree by giving her the family’s generational name.

These revelations influenced her understanding of kinship; recognizing both the profound comfort of discovering biological mirrors (i.e. her high cheekbones) and the realization that while “blood is thicker than water, love is thicker than blood,” Hollee dedicated her life to researching and building critical support structures for intercountry adoptees. But stepping into motherhood brought a new emotional dimension to questions of identity she thought she had settled, questions surrounding the inheritance and legacy of “not knowing” that were compounded by recent health crises with breast cancer. She notes that even though international adoptions from Korea are ending, “the legacy of international adoption will stretch far into the future,” explaining how “everything I don’t know, my children won’t know and their children won’t know.” Today, much of her work and research is in understanding the life course and intergenerational impact of adoption, retaining what she can for those future generations.

title: I Was the “Replacement” Baby | Through The Fog
description:
Adopted from Korea into a small-town Connecticut family, Tanya Kaanta grew up navigating displacement, family instability, and the devastating discovery that she was a “switched baby” whose adoption records belonged to another child. Despite years of bureaucratic obstacles and personal hardship, she found support through school, social work, and therapy, eventually pursuing graduate studies in social work informed by her experiences as a transracial adoptee.

After a debilitating battle with Lyme disease and autoimmune encephalitis left her facing years of physical and neurological rehabilitation, Tanya credits her children with helping her find her way forward. Today, alongside her husband of 25 years, she leads The Ties Program, an adoptee-owned heritage travel organization offering guided trips for adoptees and their loved ones, facilitated by social workers, therapists, and adult adoptees.

title: We Were Never Just “Lucky”: The Reality of Korean Adoption | Through The Fog
description:
Crossing a generational divide of forty years and entirely distinct eras of international adoption, Thomas Park Clement, a Korean War-era biracial adoptee, philanthropist, and lifelong inventor, joins Youngsun, Korean American Story’s Director of Production, for a reflective dialogue on the evolving contours of the Korean adoptee experience. Their conversation speaks to the varied, all-consuming, and all-encompassing traumas of being occupied with survival in many forms, from navigating the bomb-stricken landscape of a belligerent peninsula, to developing heightened senses of emotional perception in childhood to secure personal wellbeing.

Moving beyond antiquated narratives of rescue and gratitude, the pair delves into the history of international adoption to articulate how adoptees’ traumas are symptomatic of broader institutional shortcomings.

Rather than leaving these histories to linger in the abstract, both have taken their personal experiences to outline paths for healing and advocacy. Thomas has funneled his lifelong resourcefulness into the tangible infrastructure of reunion, supplying DNA kits through initiatives like 325Kamra to help fellow adoptees bridge geographic divides in uncovering genealogical roots. Likewise, Youngsun’s work in visual storytelling has given shape to the complex psychological landscapes of displacement, building accessible spaces where those complex experiences can be seen, shared, and affirmed. Together, their ongoing work moves past reflection to construct the networks, tools, and shared spaces necessary for the broader adoptee community.

Special thanks to the Thomas and Wonsook Foundation for their generous support in making this project possible.

title: Expectations of Reunions as an Adoptee | Through The Fog
description:
Youngsun, 33, is a visual artist based in Queens, New York. Born in Seoul, they were adopted into white family living on Long Island at around 5 months old. Growing up in a predominately white community, Youngsun describes feeling “othered”: the stares, the constant questions, and an overall narrative of “fortune” that accompanied childhood reflections on adoption—one in which gratitude was to be extended bilaterally between parent and child.

In 2019, Youngsun and their family visited Korea, a trip whose emotional charting was clear-eyed, informed by stories of other adoptees whose birth search and reunion had ended gracefully. Upon arriving at Eastern Welfare, however, Youngsun was greeted by a clinical environment with a dearth in their records, far from the warm and fuzzy experience painted by others’ accounts. When they returned from the motherland trip, Youngsun received a message from the agency relaying a closed-door situation wherein the birth mother seems to have ceased communications surrounding the adoption— second abandonment of sorts, amplified by the frustrating lack of support from the agencies which facilitated adoptions themselves. 

Today, after years of creative endeavors, continued work with Korean American and adoptee communities, investigating things they experienced in childhood, Youngsun notes that giving self-permission to grieve, in their own way, was what was most liberating: knowing that the sorrow between birth mother and child is shared; knowing that self-love and compassion comes closest to a birth mother’s love; and hoping that adoptees know there’s no right or wrong way to approach their adoption, other than staying true to their needs and intuition.

title: Finding Purpose as an Korean Adoptee | Through the Fog
description:
Adam Goodman is a 44-year-old Korean adoptee, lifelong Yankees fan, and dedicated community leader based in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Born in South Korea, he was adopted alongside his younger brother in 1986 by an American family living in Westchester County, New York. Growing up in the 80s/90s as a transracial adoptee in a predominately white area, he describes his immediate community as “colorblind,” though his parents never hid the fact of his and his brother’s adoption, mindful that they were raising Asian children in a white family. 

His childhood was busy: he was a gifted athlete, talented singer, and an honor roll student, a cocktail of achievements he partly attributes to the internal and external pressures that manifested, for him, from a sense of abandonment. On reflecting on the complex psychology of adoption, Adam notes how many adoptees may feel, and deal uniquely with, a sense of ambiguous loss; for him, this meant excelling as his mental health took a toll throughout his young adult years.

The need to excel, driven by anxiety, slowly transformed into a sense of purpose towards others. A pivotal moment arrived in 2007 when Adam attended IKAA for the first time, attending emotionally resonant panels with other adoptees with whom Adam felt a shared sense of purpose in “getting to know each other, or at least be together.” He’d go on to travel to Amsterdam for small gatherings amongst adoptees, as well as grow involved in local adoptee communities as well. 

Today, Adam serves as the Director of Youth and Teen Mentorship for @also.known.asinc, where he strives to give young people the opportunity to be a part of a larger adoptee community as they navigate various parts of their personal journeys.

title: How a Non-Korean Upbringing Affects Adoptees in America (ft. Abby Smith & Maddy Park)
description:
Bridging a rural Michigan upbringing with the fast-paced transition of moving from Korea to the United States, Abby Smith (@aejlsmith) and Maddy Park (@cafemaddy) unpack the winding paths they’ve taken as a Korean adoptee and a 1.5-generation immigrant towards calling themselves Korean American. As the pair compare notes on cultural roundedness, the frictions of belonging, and navigating racial assumptions, they contemplate on how their shared passion for digital media creation facilitated their respective journeys of affirming a sense of Korean American identity. 

Creating and consuming video content that captured the world around them—and, perhaps, how they were situated within it—was second nature: Maddy, whose father worked at a camera company, found a hobby in recording videos on camcorder, and Abby, influenced by “OG” Asian YouTubers such as Jenn Im and Michelle Phan, documented her own life while also seeing “someone who kinda looked like me… and a picture of life beyond my small town.”

The transition from creating media as a hobby to using it as a way to explore Korean American identity coincided with large transitions in their own lives. Maddy shares the surreal milestone of realizing her years were evenly split between her life in Korea and the United States, while also dealing with a move that took her from New York to a quieter town for her dental residency. Learning to cook Korean food became a way to actively sustain a connection to her roots (and destress from an intense program), while documenting it extended that feeling of healing and groundedness. 

Abby, who since having moved to New York has began questioning what being Korean American means to her as a Korean adoptee, was encouraged by her friends to document this chapter of her life: living with two Korean roommates, in the Big Apple, as she prepares for her first trip to Korea.

title: What it Means to "Return Home" as a Korean Adoptee (ft. Abby Smith)
description:
Abby Smith, 27, was born in South Korea and adopted when she was 8 months old by an American family living in rural Michigan. She grew up with two older brothers with whom she loved to spend time outside, painting a picture of a childhood set on a farm with an acreage of woods as her backyard. She describes her parents as being open to having conversations about adoption when she sought it out—they would celebrate her “Gotcha Day” alongside her birthday—though she tells us that it wasn’t a topic she often brought up.

In 2019 Abby moved to New York for work, where she met her now-roommate. She opted to stay in the city throughout Thanksgiving week when she was invited to her roommate’s Friendsgiving dinner, which, in retrospect, Abby believes was the first time she ate Korean food. Living and working in New York, where she could enter spaces that were predominately Asian American, she realized that she could likewise show up as a Korean adoptee without fear of “being outed” or judgement. She is also in community with other Korean adoptees, to whom she feels grateful for their advice on navigating through personal histories, as well as their words of wisdom on visiting Korea. 

She acknowledges the emotional apprehension around delving into one’s adoption history, while also wondering how one could ever know when they’re ready to initiate that process; “I’m going to be more emotional than I am expecting,” she says, “…but within a few years I think I’ll be able to handle it more.” Today, as Abby prepares to visit the country for the first time, she suspects that her younger self would be both excited and humbled by the all that she couldn’t have ever imagined would happen.

title: Are You Angry All the Time? A Korean Adoptee Answers | Through The Fog
description:
From stinky cabbage dishes and ceiling fan trauma, to Mr. Rogers and parenthood, friends (and puppeteering colleagues! Ed Pokropski (@epopski) and Kathy Kim (@kafode) sit down for a chat on navigating through topics which often go unspoken, like adoption and loss, and the relationships that are borne out of the trust to ask and receive questions with our loved ones. Though the pair share much in common—Korean Americans puppeteering children’s television are few and far between!—they paint a candid picture of how they’ve learned to hold conversations about the unique, and at times confusing, experiences they’ve gone through; as Kathy tells us, “Not talking about it doesn’t take it away!”

For Ed, this has taken the form of equipping himself with the tools to handle those “awkward questions” which arise in his comedy show, sharing his adoption story while taking care not to indict any question as right or wrong, but rather as a moment to illustrate that there seems to be commonalities in what non-adoptees want to understand about his experience as a transracial adoptee. As a survivor of breast cancer, Kathy describes wading through awkward interactions of a different kind, though she notes how in her experience, questions asked with the subject’s wellbeing in mind can be a relief from the choreography of pleasantries. Together, they ask each other (and themselves!) questions that might elucidate the other’s experience: Is it helpful or condescending to explain cultural concepts in the flow of conversation? How has the trendiness of all things Korean shaped the ability to grow and lean into the culture? Does Ed prefer kimchi or sauerkraut?

title: How This Emmy Nominated Korean Adoptee Is Shaping His Own Narrative | Through The Fog
description:
Edward Pokropski (@epopski) is a two-time Emmy nominated writer, producer, and comedian based in New York City, where he works at NBC and serves as an executive of Asian Comedy Fest. An avid storyteller, Ed shares that he was born in Seoul, South Korea “as far as he knows,” a caveat he uses to bring non-adoptees into the fold of his personal experiences as a transracial Korean adoptee. When he was 19 months old, Ed was adopted by a Polish-American family which, at the time, was living in California. He invokes his caveat once more when telling us of his first meal in his parents’ home—a banana with a bowl of rice—a memory which he keeps alive by eating bananas and rice in some form every year on his adoption day.

He credits his mother for trying to create safety for their family, and his younger brother, who was also adopted from Korea, for getting him to begin exploring parts of his identity as a Korean American transracial adoptee. Safety, as Ed describes, was the feeling of being accepted as your “whole self,” which he learned to articulate and express through storytelling for both adoptee and non-adoptee audiences. Whenever he takes to the stage (as with his solo show, “Case 84: Adopted in the U.S.A.”), he wants mixed audiences to be able to locate moments of resonance, understanding, and humor in stories about adoptee experiences, challenging those who might feel as though they have no connection to adoption to find within different stories glimpses of the familiar. Ultimately, Ed hopes that his shows feel like an embrace to his community.

title: The Strive to Help Those Who Need Help the Most | Legacy Project
description:
Jimmy Kim is the General Manager of LA’s Department of Recreation and Parks where he overseas the department’s recreational, social, and cultural programming. Raised in Koreatown, Jimmy recalls his youth as one challenged by street life in a rapidly changing neighborhood, telling us that he often ran with the wrong crowd. It was through his sister that he learned of the city’s summer youth employment program, which not only kept him occupied (and away from bad influences), but piqued his interests in a career working for the city’s park district.

That summer, Jimmy worked as a junior lifeguard. When the park entered its off-season, he landed a job as an attendant at E.G. Roberts Aquatic Center. Soon thereafter he again found lifeguarding positions, and, despite not being the strongest swimmer, worked tirelessly to make sure he could fulfill what the role required of him. Along the way, he rallied young folks in whom he saw bits of his own difficult past, encouraging them to join lifeguarding (as he himself had) to change their trajectories. 

In 2005, Jimmy stepped into emergency management, having learned through his role in the aquatics division how to create and act on emergency planning, and in 2015 he became an emergency manager for the park district. He played a critical role in the city’s disaster response during the COVID-19 pandemic; when much of the city’s operations slowed down, his department remained open, providing sheltering, critical care, as well as third spaces for children who needed access to online services for remote learning. In 2022, Jimmy became the first Asian American to serve as General Manager, and he remains driven by the conviction that the services provided are essential to the survival and growth of the city’s most vulnerable communities.

title: The Importance of Relationships and the Willingness to Never Stop Learning (ft. Connie Chung)
description:
Connie Chung is a second-generation Korean American urban planner and a managing partner at the consulting firm HR&A Advisors. Born in Los Angeles and raised in the Pacific Palisades during the 1980s, Connie’s upbringing was defined by a strong sense of community; she tells us that though the Palisades weren’t as popular with Korean folks back in the day, her family found a welcoming and sweet neighborhood where everyone knew one another.

Her professional journey has been shaped by experiences working across urban development, community resilience, and public policy, ranging from post-Hurricane Sandy economic recovery to the revitalization of Boston’s Lawn on D. Connie’s expertise in climate resilience planning took on a personal dimension when the Pacific Palisades Fire impacted her parents’ home. The experience gave her a profound, up-close understanding of the systemic challenges—from insurance negotiations to the psychological burden of disaster survival—that residents increasingly face in an era of accelerating climate change. 

Today, as managing partner of her firm’s L.A. office, Connie focuses on mission-driven consultancy, addressing critical urban issues like housing, homelessness, and the creation of open spaces. She is a staunch advocate for environmental justice, particularly regarding the dangers of extreme heat, which she views as a pervasive and less invisible consequence of climate change. Whether she is advocating for urban greening or addressing critical housing needs, Connie remains committed to the principle that professional success is rooted in the deeply personal ability to connect “one-on-one with people and understand them in their wholeness.”

title: How Culture is Preserved Through Community (ft. Kaylee Cho)
description:
Kaylee Cho is the Climate Resilience Specialist at Koreatown Youth and Community Center (KYCC), where she works with KYCC’s Environmental Services Unit to address challenges at the intersection of public health, environmental justice, and community advocacy in Los Angeles. For Kaylee, a lifelong Angeleno who has been involved with the organization since her youth, working as a climate resilience specialist has been, in her words, a “full-circle moment” where she could leverage her personal interests and education in the service of her community.

Her work is deeply informed by personal experience, having witnessed the impact which environmental and systemic stressors has left on her own family. Whether through her research at Breathe Southern California or her advocacy for tenant rights, Kaylee has serves as a voice for those living in Koreatown’s high-density, renter-heavy landscape, where invisible dangers like mold and poor air quality often go unaddressed due to a lack of resources or fear of landlord retaliation. 

By focusing on the social determinants of health, Kaylee pushes for systems-level change, from the electrification of aging infrastructure to the creation of accessible green spaces. Her approach is rooted in empathy: a commitment to meeting community members where they are, ensuring that the pursuit of climate justice is realized and reflected in the health of community members. She hopes to one day go to graduate school to undertake research in community health before returning to the nonprofit sector.

Whether through her research at Breathe Southern California or her advocacy for tenant rights, Kaylee has serves as a voice for those living in Koreatown’s high-density, renter-heavy landscape, where invisible dangers like mold and poor air quality often go unaddressed due to a lack of resources or fear of landlord retaliation. 

By focusing on the social determinants of health, Kaylee pushes for systems-level change, from the electrification of aging infrastructure to the creation of accessible green spaces. Her approach is rooted in empathy: a commitment to meeting community members where they are, ensuring that the pursuit of climate justice is realized and reflected in the health of community members. She hopes to one day go to graduate school to undertake research in community health before returning to the nonprofit sector.

title: Advice on How to Be Successful in a Growing, Diverse Community (ft. Billy Yoon)
description:
Billy Yoon is the current owner and steward of Koreana Gifts and Arts, a legacy boutique shop in Los Angeles selling vintage Korean crafts. He was born in Inglewood, California, to a family whose legacy is deeply intertwined with that of Korean American history in the 20th century; his maternal grandfather, Choong Sup Park, left Korea under Japanese occupation to work in the sugarcane plantations of Hawaii before arriving in Riverside at the invitation of the activist Dosan Ahn Chang-ho. His paternal grandfather, Kyung Hak Yoon, worked as a migrant farmer as one of the first Koreans to immigrate directly through San Francisco in 1903.

Raised in the “midtown” neighborhood of 1960s Los Angeles—southwest of today’s Koreatown—Billy recalls growing up during a point in L.A.’s history when the entire Korean community was centered on a single block near Jefferson Boulevard, where one of the earliest Korean American churches still stands to this day. Although the city boasts a large Korean American community today, Billy notes that this was not the case in his youth.

After a pivotal decision to withdraw from a medical path in college, he pursued a degree in the arts, eventually dedicating fifteen years to teaching art in public schools. In 2003, he transitioned from education to business, taking over the store which he used to frequent as a child with his mother. Today, he manages what is arguably the world’s largest collection of vintage Korean dolls, as well as other hand-painted wooden pieces and traditional instruments. For Billy, life is an ongoing act of curation and conversation, believing that every person we encounter holds a piece of knowledge we have yet to discover. “One of the great things about LA,” he reminds us, “is that we have everybody here.”

title: Pachinko Writer Soo Hugh on Being the Only Korean in the Room | Legacy Project
description:
Soo Hugh is a New York-based showrunner, producer, and television writer whose filmography includes AMC’s “The Terror,” ABC’s “The Whispers,” and Apple TV+’s “Pachinko,” adapted from Min Jin Lee’s novel of the same name. Born in Busan, South Korea, in 1977, she moved to the suburbs of Maryland when she was a one-year old, growing up alongside her brother as self-described “latchkey kids” who helped their parents run their deli—or as they say in Maryland, a “carry-out.” 

Between the downtime afforded to her by her parents’ busy schedules, Soo developed a love for stories and storytelling—first in letters, and later in motion pictures through Francis Coppola’s “The Godfather.”Her work is characterized by what she calls a “shock of recognition:” that deeply human moment in which a profoundly electric connection is established between self and subject, a relationship  that transcends spatial and temporal bounds. From 19th-century British Royal Navy sailors (The Terror) to the resilient women living through the Japanese occupation of Korea, Soo inhabits, transforms, and imbues life into the characters through whom she hopes to “talk to a world.” 

Today, Soo views the storytelling muscle as a vital human tool, one that demands we step into the skin of others to foster a kinder world. Whether speaking to a new generation of writers or raising her own children, she champions the belief that we are not tied to the realities we are born into; through storytelling, one has the ability to render their world in empathy.

title: Coming Out To Our Christian Korean American Parents with Patience and Understanding

title: Words of Advice for those Afraid to Express Their True Self (ft. Jiwon Shin)
description:
Jiwon Shin is a New York-based nightlife and event performer. Born in Highland Park, a suburb of Chicago, she grew up between Kentucky and Los Angeles, following her mother after her parents’ divorce. In the years which she describes as “a crack in the mirror,” Jiwon found a lifeline in music and the precise, expressive choreography of imported K-pop VHS tapes such as SBS’ Inkigayo (인기가요) and MBC’s Show! Music Core (쇼! 음악중심). More than just play, these living-room dances were staged performances in which Jiwon would recruit her brothers to form their own little K-pop group, in which each sibling was cast as a particular member of a group. 

With her mother’s encouragement, Jiwon would later move to New York City to pursue studies in fashion business management at FIT, which is where she began to step out of her comfort zone. She found that experimentation with how she presented herself proved to be the formula for getting invited to perform music and drag, with her debut happening in 2019 to outstanding success. 

Since then, Jiwon has emerged as a breakout force in the Brooklyn queer community, using drag and K-pop performance art as tools for personal and collective affirmation; today, Jiwon champions a "chosen family" of fellow performers, viewing the stage as a sanctuary where the healing of an inner child and the celebration of modern queer culture converge to create something entirely new and electric. “You only have one life and you have to live it like your authentic self,” she tells us, “…if you don’t do that, you’re going to live for everybody else. And what kind of life is that?”

title: Mental Health in Korean Families and the Difficult Conversations That Follow | Legacy Project
description:
Marina Lee was born around Seoul, South Korea, and moved to Philadelphia when she was four years old with her parents and two older brothers. Her memories of Korea are centered around the unconditional love of her parents, as well as her mother’s legendary cooking, which drew the attention of neighbors who’d “invite” themselves over to Marina’s home for a taste of what her mother had prepared. Every week, it seemed, her family would inevitably host a dinner party for her parents’ friends and families. From dinner parties to rituals of making kimchi with her mother (and other ahjummas), Marina tells us that she holds not a single negative memory of life before moving to the United States.

When Marina was four-years old, her father, an accountant for the US Army, was offered the chance to relocate his family to Philadelphia following the surprise recovery of a sum of money. In the midst of adjusting to immigrant life in her town—where she was the only person of color in her Kindergarten class—Marina began noticing the slow and confusing deterioration of her mother’s mental health: the self-talk, the changing nature of food on the table, and the growing emotional distance in the household. Yet in the face of a new country, where assimilation rhetoric and stigma surrounding mental health prohibited open discussion, Marina was left at a loss for how she could nurse her mother back to health, freeing her from an illness which trapped her in her own mind. 

When she was a teenager, she recounts how, in a rare moment of lucidity, her mother apologized to her for her condition, cementing Marina’s conviction to continue fighting for her mother. After graduating from college, she took it upon herself to learn as much as she could about her mother’s schizophrenia, whereupon she learned through other physical screenings that her mother was afflicted by several other health issues as well. Although she was able to provide treatment for her mother which improved her mental health, her mother would pass at the young age of 65. 

Today, with a daughter of her own, Marina admits that she is “overly communicative,” though she urges families—particularly those from different cultural backgrounds—to have open conversations about mental health and wellbeing. Her advice for her daughter? “Don’t take life so seriously, have some fun, have a lot of fun, because you only have one.”

title: How the Bravery of One Man Saved a Family from Certain Death (ft. John Young Ho Lee)
description:
John Young Ho Lee was born on June 25, 1936, in Pocheon, Korea. Born into a landed, “yangban” (aristocratic) family, he recalls how village folk would refer to him as “doryeon-nim” (young master), in place of his own name. He tells us that he lived comfortably, and even had hospitable relations with Japanese soldiers who would occasionally stroll into his town on horseback, with his mother preparing them Korean food which they seemed to like. 

His father, along with his uncle, had received police training in Japan (serving in the Japanese police force), and continued working for the police upon his return to Korea. As part of the landed class, his family allotted plots of land to sharecroppers who gave them their harvest. After liberation, however, his family had a reversal of fortune: their land was taken and redistributed by the Communist Party, and they had to go into hiding after villagers alerted party officials to his family’s status as landlords; he remembers hiding in his family’s cornfields as their former tenants sought them out. Young Ho and his family found refuge in Sinwi, though not before he learned of his grandparents’ abduction by the party. 

In time, he would graduate from law school before working as an accountant for the U.S. Eighth Army for 24 years, with stints in Saudi Arabia. In 1980, he was granted papers to immigrate to the United States, where he and his wife hoped to give their children better educations. Today, he enjoys spending time with his grandchildren—and the feelings are reciprocated.

title: Experiencing Loneliness in What Should be a Time of Joy | Letters to My Hometown
description:
Reverend David Jungdo Park grew up in Madeok, Hwanghae Province (today known as “Yeomjeon” in South Hwanghae Province, North Korea) during a tumultuous era of Korean history: born nine years before liberation, he still remembers the song he sang as a schoolboy after hearing of the emperor’s surrender. His father having passed before liberation, David was raised by his mother alongside his sister, Yeon-do, who, at the time of recording, he has not seen since leaving his hometown 78 years ago. 

In his conversation with his grandson, John, Reverend Park speaks to moments from his childhood whose values he carried with him to the present day: earnest faith, which his mother shared with him through Korean readings of the Bible during Japanese occupation, and stewardship, which he learned from his father as he tended to his orchards, transplanting saplings, pruning and grafting branches.

Like so many elders interviewed for this iteration of Letters to My Hometown, Reverend Park embodies that tree which has been pruned, transplanted, and nurtured to bear fruit in the stories he has to share (John notes how the both of them share a predisposition towards storytelling). Often, these stories are held in waiting by the elder generation, whose preoccupation with raising their own children in a foreign environment takes urgent precedence over the recollection of past experiences, stories, and traumas. 

Yet in time the stories emerge, prompting younger generations—the grandchildren of these elders—to find in these testimonies a storied link to their roots, and to their hometowns; a single family, grafted and propagated an ocean away.

The 75 years of division and conflict from the Korean War have not only affected the first generation, who still long for their hometowns in North Korea, but also younger generations who have no memories of the conflict, yet many of whom have inherited the weight of uncertainty and the mission of searching for missing relatives.

This iteration of Letters to My Hometown invites audiences to listen and reflect upon intergenerational conversations of the Korean American community whose divided families have sustained the traumas of their homeland’s partition. Generously supported by American Friends Service Committee, these conversations aim to take steps toward transforming the intergenerational traumas of the Korean War into opportunities for collective remembering, learning, and healing.

title: The Commitment to Faith Through Discrimination and War | Legacy Project
description:
Reverend David Jungdo Park was born in Madeok, Hwanghae Province, in 1936. Raised in a family that had been early adherents of Christianity on the Korean Peninsula, David became accustomed with both the Korean alphabet as well as the Christian faith through bible readings with his mother, which, at the time of Japanese occupation, was considered an illicit activity. He recounts how his father, beaten by Japanese authorities, did not survive to see liberation on August 15, 1945, a day he distinctly remembers as being filled with trumpeters marching throughout the streets as townsfolk cheered “manseh!” Yet after only a couple months of liberation, David’s life was again thrown into disarray when the North Korean government enacted policies which disrupted Christian life.

In the winter of 1950-51, the Armed Defense Unit which had held the line against encroaching Chinese and North Korean forces splintered and was forced to retreat; David’s uncle, who had been a member of the unit, warned his family to flee before the soldiers arrived, though he himself was killed in combat. As David’s grandfather, an elder of the town, would have been unable to make this journey, David’s mother and sister opted to return to their hometown to be with him.

title: Recalling the First Experience of Separation from Family (feat. David Jungdo Park)
description:
Reverend David Jungdo Park was born in Madeok, Hwanghae Province, in 1936. Raised in a family that had been early adherents of Christianity on the Korean Peninsula, David became accustomed with both the Korean alphabet as well as the Christian faith through bible readings with his mother, which, at the time of Japanese occupation, was considered an illicit activity. title: The Importance of Sharing and Reflecting on War with Others (feat. Sun Ok Hwang)
description:
Sun Ok Hwang was born in Shinchon, Hwanghae Province on February 13th, 1935, her earliest memories being of life under Japanese occupation. Her father, Jin Seop Hwang, joined their fire department’s night patrol to avoid being a target of the Japanese military’s arbitrary arrests while her mother, Young Sun Choi, would silently pick up rice from farmers whose harvest were to be taken by the Japanese. 

Sun Ok tells us that her hometown was surrounded by fertile, arable land with productive rice fields that could only be enjoyed by the local Koreans illicitly; even then, as the Japanese had taken away their metallic dinnerware, many families had to eat with wooden, earthenware, or ceramic bowls. There was little time for celebration after liberation as her hometown was then partitioned as part of Communist Korea, whose ruling party imprisoned her father multiple times before he eventually passed from illness and repeated abuse.

In the midst of the Korean War, Sun Ok was taken to Ongjin, on the very edge of Hwanghae Province, by her grandfather, after which she crossed the 38th parallel to Baeknyun-do, an island off the coast of Incheon with a heavy American naval presence. From there she went to Busan, where she stayed for a year, before coming to Seoul, where a relative of her mother was stationed. She attended and graduated from college, after which she worked as a teacher’s assistant before meeting and marrying her husband In Whan Rheem, who had his own experiences of leaving his hometown in the North during the war. 

She finds that being with someone with shared experienced allowed for the two to better understand and support one another as they navigated life both in South Korea, and then in the United States, as those who left their hometown and family in the North. Today, she’s grateful for her children, whose faith and lives she takes pride in, as well as her grandchildren.

title: What a True "Home" Means with a Network of Love | Letters to My Hometown
description:
Daniel Han and his mother, Sue Rheem, are joined in dialogue by Daniel’s grandparents, In Whan Rheem and Sun Ok Hwang, as they reflect on all that their family had endured, witnessed, and overcome. A truly intergenerational conversation that touches upon how Korea’s tumultuous modern history disrupted familial relationships, the In Whan Rheem and Sun Ok Hwang describe life under Japanese occupation, where the elder Rheem’s father was imprisoned for dissident activity, and how his wife, Noh Gi-bok, would tend to him in prison despite the soldiers’ berating. They also speak on what people lost during the Korean War: jobs and homes, yes, but also family and whimsy.

Now, fifty years since leaving Korea, Mrs. Hwang notes that she feels no urgency to “return” home, instead choosing to adapt to the present. Sue Rheem feels similarly; for her, family is home, her sense of self attached not to a particular time or place, but with her loved ones, or, as Mrs. Hwang would say, their “network of love.” In documenting these conversations, the Rheem family tells us how even when our family histories contain episodes of displacement and unimaginable loss, the sanctuary of a family’s devotion remains grounded in the hometown that travels with them, one constituted not of soil but of stories and those who pass them along.

The 75 years of division and conflict from the Korean War have not only affected the first generation, who still long for their hometowns in North Korea, but also younger generations who have no memories of the conflict, yet many of whom have inherited the weight of uncertainty and the mission of searching for missing relatives.

This iteration of Letters to My Hometown invites audiences to listen and reflect upon intergenerational conversations of the Korean American community whose divided families have sustained the traumas of their homeland’s partition. Generously supported by American Friends Service Committee, these conversations aim to take steps toward transforming the intergenerational traumas of the Korean War into opportunities for collective remembering, learning, and healing.

title: A Journey to Peace Through Martyrdom and Mercy | Legacy Project
description:
In Whan Rheem was born on November 12th, 1928 near Pyongyang, raised in a pastoral family where faith and education were deeply intertwined. Despite a frail childhood that delayed his start in school, he would go on to study at the prestigious Pyongyang High School before attending college and later seminary, honoring his family’s insistence that he complete his college education before entering the ministry. His early years were shaped by the constraints of Japanese occupation—where the Korean language was relegated to a single weekly lesson—and the profound joy of liberation.

The peace of liberation soon gave way to the terrors of the Korean War as ideological machinations tore the country apart. Rheem suffered the devastating loss of both his father and older brother, who were martyred for their faith; he later discovered his father’s body among the mass burial pits at Yongsan, a sight that solidified his resolve to flee to the south. He recalls his journey as one teetering on the precipice of death: a forty-day walk to Seoul, a perilous ride on the roof of a train to Busan where refugees who tired would fall onto the rails, and a period of near-starvation in Jeju where he eventually found work teaching at a refugee school.

Seeking a life free from the perpetual state of conflict that plagued his homeland, Rheem moved his ministry to Canada, which he says “felt like ‘heaven’ for its promise of food and freedom,” before eventually being sponsored to settle in the United States. Now, reflecting on a journey marked by both martyrdom and mercy, he offers his legacy as a spiritual compass for his descendants, praying that future generations maintain their faith while upholding and cherishing one another.

title: The True Sacrifice of Parents for their Children (ft. Michelle Kim Rogers)
description:
Michelle Kim Rogers was born in Seoul in 1961, her early years divided between the discipline of her uncle’s home and the rustic warmth of her grandmother’s farm in Icheon. While her parents worked to establish a foothold in the United States, Michelle spent her childhood in Korea drinking fresh goat milk and wearing hand-knit wool leggings, envisions the United States as a place where “dollar bills were plastered on walls.” 

When she finally reunited with her parents in Salt Lake City in 1970 after years of separation, the fantasy was instantly replaced by a sharp realization of the financial and emotional cost of the American Dream. Seeing her mother’s aged face at the airport, Michelle understood that her family’s new life was built not on luck, but on grueling labor in sewing factories and years of disciplined saving.

Her journey through the American landscape—from Utah road trips in an un-air-conditioned Ford LTD to the racial bullying she faced on New Jersey school buses—was anchored by her parents' resilience and the unexpected kindness offered to her by strangers. 

Today, Michelle’s story has come full circle through her work with the International Institute of New England, where she co-sponsors and mentors refugee families seeking to establish their own foothold in America. Working with those in whom she sees her family’s early American selves, she emphasizes the necessity of kindness and generosity in supporting our immigrant neighbors, affirming that the true wealth of the American experience stems from our ability to show up for the most vulnerable.

title: Piecing the World Together from Grandfather's Eyes | Letters to My Hometown
description:
Tae-hyok Kim is joined by his children, Michelle and Harold, as well as his granddaughter Nicole, in a conversation on the archival, therapeutic, and familial importance of passing down stories. For Tae, the story began seventy-seven years ago when he left his village, Cheong-duk-gol, for Seoul, not realizing that his departure from home would become permanent amidst the backdrop of the Korean War. Embedded into this story are accounts of cold, harsh winters which prevented his family from collectively crossing into the South, alongside memories of home-cooked meals shared with family in his rural farming community.

This history, once a series of detailed stories told during a long family drive from Utah to New Jersey, served both as an anchoring point for his children and grandchildren’s identities, as well as reparative acts of therapy for Tae-hyok himself. An enthusiastic writer, Tae-hyok typed out his life experiences across hundreds of pages, though in 2018, a stroke left Tae-hyeok with a significant speech impairment, fundamentally changing how he communicated but not his determination to share his legacy. During the pandemic, Nicole interviewed him for thirty minutes a day to fill the gaps in his original manuscripts, determined to understand her grandfather and the world he navigated, transforming family lore into something permanently legible and accessible for others to read.

Through their collaboration, they produced a book which captured Tae’s central philosophy: that one must always have a goal, but also a dream—because once a goal is achieved, the dream becomes the next goal to pursue. Today, the family views their history not as a fading memory, but as a documented testament to endurance. Together, Michelle, Harold, and Nicole express gratitude to Tae-Hyok for never ceasing to share his story with them.

title: Conclusions of War From a Korean War Survivor's Perspective | Letters to My Hometown
description:
Won Yun is joined in conversation by his daughter-in-law Cristina, and his granddaughter, Emily, in a reflection on the enduring cost of war and the fragile threads of family connection. Born before the outbreak of the war in North Korea, Won’s childhood in Pyongyang was a landscape of contrast, where the joy of skating on the frozen Daedong River was eventually eclipsed by the nightly raids of the Korean War. 

At ten years old, he survived a B-29 bombing by sheltering in a sewer hole; when he emerged, he discovered that those in the neighboring bunker had not survived. During the retreat south, he was tossed alone into a boat to cross the river, refusing to move from the far bank until the boatman returned for his father and brother.

Yet the victory of their escape was shadowed by the sisters left behind—a separation that left his parents in a state of lifelong mourning. Decades later, Won traveled back to the North for a brief, shadowed reunion in a motel room monitored by hidden cameras. Forbidden from speaking freely, he and his sisters communicated through handwritten notes to bridge the decades of separation, asking in secret if they still held to their father’s faith and the shared memories of their youth. 

After flushing those fragile testimonies to protect their safety, Won returned home with a story he now preserves as a "time capsule" for future generations. Now 84, he offers his journey as an urgent prayer that his grandchildren might live in a world where peace is a permanent reality.

The 75 years of division and conflict from the Korean War have not only affected the first generation, who still long for their hometowns in North Korea, but also younger generations who have no memories of the conflict, yet many of whom have inherited the weight of uncertainty and the mission of searching for missing relatives.

This iteration of Letters to My Hometown invites audiences to listen and reflect upon intergenerational conversations of the Korean American community whose divided families have sustained the traumas of their homeland’s partition. Generously supported by American Friends Service Committee, these conversations aim to take steps toward transforming the intergenerational traumas of the Korean War into opportunities for collective remembering, learning, and healing.

title: The Shocking Transition from Survival to True Happiness | Legacy Project
description:
​​Won Yun was born in 1942 in Sariwon, Hwanghae Province, later moving to Pyongyang where his ministerial father was called to serve. He spent a childhood filled with simple joys, like skating on the frozen Daedong River and eating his grandmother’s mung bean pancakes and naengmyeon, foods representative of his locale. 

This peace was shattered during the January 4th retreat, when Won was separated from half his family and narrowly survived a B-29 bombing by hiding under a manhole—emerging to find that those in the underground shelter he couldn't enter had not survived. After years of hardship in refugee camps, where his family often had to scavenge and boil scraps left by American GIs, Won moved to Daegu and finally to Seoul, where he met his wife in a church choir.

In 1965, Won arrived in Los Angeles with $100 and a one-way plane ticket bought by a family friend. He began his American life as a midnight dishwasher in Chinatown, often walking two hours home after his shift, until a move to New Jersey allowed him to finally practice architecture. The arrival of his wife in 1967 and their honeymoon at Niagara Falls marked the definitive transition from survival to a new chapter of happiness, heralded by newfound friends, a growing family, and a used Ford Galaxy. 

Looking back on eighty years, Won views his life through the lens of his grandfather’s wisdom: that in a world of uncertainty, a person’s greatest assets are the good friends they choose to walk with. He wishes for his grandchildren to cherish their friendships, who might accompany them in their own lives.

title: The Sacrifices, Regrets and Triumphs of Raising a Korean Family in America (ft. Chung Kun Lim)
description:
Chung Kun Lim was born in 1944 in Jeonju, her childhood shaped by the displacement of the Korean War and the constant threat of bombings. As the seventh of eight daughters, she was raised under strict discipline in a society that traditionally prioritized male heirs—a reality she felt deeply when her mother’s hard-won educational legacy was eventually inherited by male relatives rather than the daughters who helped build it. A talented soprano, Chung Kun majored in vocal music at Sookmyung Women’s University—she jokes about how all her crying must have trained her vocal chords—before immigrating to the United States in 1966.

In America, she traded her musical aspirations for the back-breaking, restless work of dry cleaning; by her estimate, she and her husband likely opened one of the first Korean-owned dry cleaners in the country. While this relentless labor secured her children's education and success, it came at the cost of their mother tongue, a linguistic gap she regrets. 

Yet when reflecting on her years of "meaningful hardship," Chung Kun views her children’s character as her true inheritance, saying, “they’ve met wonderful partners, and are kind to us… I have nothing more to ask for.” Today, she finds peace in the knowledge that her sacrifices paved the path for her children’s lives in America, giving thanks to God for her health and strength throughout the years.

title: The Difficulties of Growing Up Korean in America | Letters to My Hometown
description:
In a conversation between parents and daughter which is at once raw, poignant, and hopeful, Rosa Kwon sits down for a heart-to-heart with her parents, David and Jean Yoon Kwon, to navigate the untranslated geography of their family’s history. While David and Jean Yoon departed from Pyeongyang and Shinuiju at an early age—their respective hometowns north of the 38th parallel—their candid and clarifying conversation with Rosa reveals how the greatest distance they’ve traveled isn’t across borders, but across the dining table. 

For the senior Kwons, whose lives have encompassed Japanese occupation, the Korean War, and the oppressive Yushin regime of 1970s South Korea, emigration to the United States necessitated a singular focus on survival. Yet in the pursuit of the American dream, their heritage was eclipsed by the immediate demands of the present; in its place, a cultural and linguistic tension where Rosa has felt perpetually viewed through the lens of a seven-year-old, and a regret for what parents left lost in translation.

The family explores the friction between Rosa’s desire to reconnect with her heritage and her parents’ questioning of such a project’s 가치, or worth. From Rosa’s perspective, conversations like the one recorded with her parents serve as reasons enough: the conversational barrier had kept parents and children from speaking candidly with each other, leading to years of miscommunicated thoughts, feelings, and expectations. But through tears and newfound honesty, they begin to dismantle the barriers built by decades of unspoken truths, showing us that while the link to the motherland may be frayed, the path toward mutual understanding can always be rewritten—one translated text and one "I love you" at a time.

The 75 years of division and conflict from the Korean War have not only affected the first generation, who still long for their hometowns in North Korea, but also younger generations who have no memories of the conflict, yet many of whom have inherited the weight of uncertainty and the mission of searching for missing relatives.

This iteration of Letters to My Hometown invites audiences to listen and reflect upon intergenerational conversations of the Korean American community whose divided families have sustained the traumas of their homeland’s partition. Generously supported by @afsc_org, these conversations aim to take steps toward transforming the intergenerational traumas of the Korean War into opportunities for collective remembering, learning, and healing.

title: The Horrors of Being a Retreating Civilian During Wartime (ft. Jean Yoon Kwon)
description:
Jean Yoon Kwon was born in Seoul, Korea, during the Japanese occupation. Although she was born in Seoul, Jean Yoon spent her early childhood in Pyongyang, where her father worked as a regional manager for a bank; she recalls playing with her siblings by the banks of the Taedong river, as well as accompanying her father on night strolls to Morangbong hill. 

A year after liberation, Jean Yoon was with her mother and newly-born brother in their family residence when Soviet soldiers barged into their home with weapons drawn. Nobody was harmed, and the next day, the family fled by boat from the coast of Haeju to arrive at Hoehyeon-dong, Seoul, where her grandfather resided. 

After the Korean War began, Jean Yoon had to flee once more during the January 4th Retreat of 1951, where she crossed a frozen Mapo river with her family before walking down the highway alongside other refugees and soldiers. She recounts the hellscape along the road as B-29 bombers flew overhead, attempting to firebomb an encroaching Chinese army which was indistinguishable from families running away from the conflict. 

Despite the chaos of the retreat, Jean Yoon’s family miraculously survived the journey south, though she maintains that the horrors she witnessed on that highway were beyond imagination.

title: Vivid Memories of Fleeing as a Civilian During the Korean War | Legacy Project
description:
Jean Yoon Kwon was born in Seoul, Korea, during the Japanese occupation. Although she was born in Seoul, Jean Yoon spent her early childhood in Pyongyang, where her father worked as a regional manager for a bank; she recalls playing with her siblings by the banks of the Taedong river, as well as accompanying her father on night strolls to Morangbong hill. 

A year after liberation, Jean Yoon was with her mother and newly-born brother in their family residence when Soviet soldiers barged into their home with weapons drawn. Nobody was harmed, and the next day, the family fled by boat from the coast of Haeju to arrive at Hoehyeon-dong, Seoul, where her grandfather resided. 

After the Korean War began, Jean Yoon had to flee once more during the January 4th Retreat of 1951, where she crossed a frozen Mapo river with her family before walking down the highway alongside other refugees and soldiers. She recounts the hellscape along the road as B-29 bombers flew overhead, attempting to firebomb an encroaching Chinese army which was indistinguishable from families running away from the conflict. 

Despite the chaos of the retreat, Jean Yoon’s family miraculously survived the journey south, though she maintains that the horrors she witnessed on that highway were beyond imagination.

title: How a Stroke of Luck Saved him from Deportation (ft. David Soon Ho Kwon)
description:
David Soon Ho Kwon was born in 1936 in Kyoto, Japan, to a mother who worked as an assistant for a Japanese aristocrat. From his early childhood years, he recalls the day-to-day discrimination faced by Koreans living in Japan, from being denied healthcare at the hospital, to being the first medics which the Japanese Empire shipped off to serve in the treacherous Pacific front. His mother, who had been certified as a nurse, was among those called to serve in the South Pacific, though she managed to get herself and David out of the country by leveraging the language skills she had acquired while working for the aristocracy to pass as Japanese.

Soon after arriving in Manchuria, David’s mother found work as a nurse in a rural hospital, where she stayed until liberation. Though they had initially fled Japan to avoid certain death, the pair found themselves having to flee once more, this time settling in Shinuiju, a Korean border town, after hearing of locals who had been killing Japanese people in retaliation (they had been passing as Japanese). They soon crossed the 38th parallel in 1946 to settle in Seoul. Much later, in 1971, David moved again, this time to the United States, to work as an engineer. 

Through every border crossed and every identity assumed, the heart of David's journey still remains the towering courage of his mother, who risked everything to ensure her son would one day no longer need to hide himself.

title: To the Father I Haven't Seen in Seventy-Five Years | Letters to My Hometown
description:
Ninety-year-old Chang Soon Lee sits before a computer to write a letter to the father he hasn't seen in seventy-five years, a man who remained a distant but precious memory after their separation during the Korean War. Joined by his children, Bora and Bob, Reverend Lee recounts the deep-rooted courage of his own father—a minister who defied Japanese authorities to protect his parish—while grappling with the silence that defined his family’s history. 

His son speaks with poignant honesty about a childhood felt in the shadow of his father’s emotional distance, yet poignantly highlights a transformative moment of reconciliation when Reverend Lee humbly asked for his forgiveness. From the streets of Pyongyang to the quiet reflections of old age, they explore the burdens of the "provider" generation and the grace found in late-life vulnerability. Together, they consider how integrity and faith are transmitted across generations, proving that even a relationship once defined by absence can evolve into a lasting legacy of character and purposeful love.

The 75 years of division and conflict from the Korean War have not only affected the first generation, who still long for their hometowns in North Korea, but also younger generations who have no memories of the conflict, yet many of whom have inherited the weight of uncertainty and the mission of searching for missing relatives.

This iteration of Letters to My Hometown invites audiences to listen and reflect upon intergenerational conversations of the Korean American community whose divided families have sustained the traumas of their homeland’s partition. Generously supported by @afsc_org, these conversations aim to take steps toward transforming the intergenerational traumas of the Korean War into opportunities for collective remembering, learning, and healing.

title: The Struggles of Displacement and the Will to Continue On | Legacy Project
description:
Born in Korea during the Japanese occupation, Reverend Chang Soon Lee reflects on a life shaped by faith, displacement, and pastoral care amid the upheavals of colonial rule, war, and migration. Raised between Pyongyang and the countryside, he recalls childhood under Japanese occupation—being punished for speaking Korean at school, forced name changes, and the terror of watching his father arrested by Japanese police during worship. Liberation brought hope, but it was quickly followed by hardship under Soviet occupation and, soon after, the devastation of the Korean War. 

In 1971, Lee arrived alone in the United States, intending to study theology before returning to Korea. Instead, an unexpected invitation to remain in Los Angeles altered the course of his life, allowing him to secure permanent residency, reunite his family, and complete advanced theological training at Claremont School of Theology. Ordained in the United Methodist Church, he went on to found and lead a Korean ministry within a multilingual, multiracial congregation, serving for more than two decades. 

Deeply shaped by the vulnerabilities of immigrants, Lee’s ministry emphasized social services, advocacy, and encouragement—particularly for those navigating immigration systems, language barriers, and moral judgment.
